extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of chemistry; readers preparing or studying an elementary chemistry treatise
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and organizing an elementary chemistry treatise, especially its pedagogical order, experimental basis, and systematic chemical nomenclature. Focuses on how to present facts, names, tables, and laboratory operations for beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceed from the known to the unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional order must go 'du connu à l'inconnu' — teach beginning learners by starting with known facts and sensations and then advancing to the unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach by following the natural generation of ideas (as in childhood): begin with observations and direct experience, then build successive linked ideas so learners can 'retrouver le fil & l'enchaînement'. Avoid starting with abstract principles that presuppose later lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base conclusions only on experiments and observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not deduce beyond what experiments present ('ne rien conclure au-delà de ce que les expériences présentent'); suppress or continually test reasoning by experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid accepting suppositions or authority-based assertions. Keep reasoning tightly tied to experimental data and use experiments to correct false judgments. The author emphasizes preventing error by subjecting claims to experience rather than speculative inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify reasoning; reduce argument to evident facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, simplify or eliminate speculative reasoning and reduce arguments to short, obvious judgments anchored in observable data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the style of mathematicians: arrange data and use simple operations so reasoning never loses sight of evident guides. The aim is to prevent long chains of inference that may mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise, exact, and meaningful language
rubrics_metrics.description: Words must carry clear ideas ('nous ne pensons qu'avec le secours des mots'); language precision is essential to correct thinking and transmission of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt terminology that evokes the most general or characteristic property of a substance; avoid names that create false ideas (e.g., 'huile', 'beurre', 'fleurs' for minerals). Prefer meaningful coinages (often from Greek) to empty or misleading traditional names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict elementary treatises to clarity and concision; avoid historical digressions
rubrics_metrics.description: An elementary work should prioritize ease, clarity, and brevity and should not burden beginners with long historical citations or exhaustive debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit extended historiography or protracted discussion of predecessors in an elementary manual; these distract and make the text tedious for novices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify substances into classes, genera, and species reflecting their composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize compounds according to natural groupings: classes (genre) name the common property, species specify differences (e.g., acids composed of an acidifying principle + a specific principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use class names to recall shared properties and specific names to indicate particular constituents. The logical progression mirrors how children generalize from individual examples to classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design nomenclature so names encode composition and state
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose names and terminations that indicate which combustible/acid/base is present, their proportions, and states of saturation so that 'par le mot seul, on reconnoît' the composition and relative excesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use changes of termination to express different states (examples: sulfuric vs. sulfurous states); construct compound names to reveal which combustible substance enters the combination and whether acid or base is in excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change established names only for lack of accepted terms or to correct misleading names
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not alter traditional names merely for novelty; change names when new substances lack settled names or when existing names produce evidently false ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substituting names, prefer ones that express the most characteristic property; adopt new terms sparingly and with reason (authors used Greek roots when appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use composite and systematic naming for multi-constituent substances
rubrics_metrics.description: For bodies formed of multiple simple substances, employ compound names and form classes to avoid disorder; for ternary compounds (e.g., neutral salts) indicate acidifying principle, acidified principle, and base in the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form uniform terminations and naming rules so that different species and states of similar salts are consistently indicated by their names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide exhaustive tables of substances and combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include organized tables listing substances simples, radicals, binary combinations (oxygen with metals/non-metals), and combinations of various acids with bases, with observations attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second part is devoted to comprehensive tabular nomenclature and combination tables, ordered by affinity or alphabetically where affinities are unknown; accompany tables with observations for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a practical operations section describing experimental methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a detailed, practice-oriented section on laboratory operations and manipulations relevant to modern chemistry so readers can perform experiments themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The third part should give detailed descriptions of operations, grouped by analogous procedures across chapters; emphasize methods drawn from the author's own experience where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not presuppose the science in early chapters; avoid introducing undefined expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid early chapters that assume knowledge or use expressions not previously defined; many texts fail beginners by treating principles before phenomena and definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with principal phenomena and definitions so novices can acquire vocabulary, apparatus familiarity, and experimental appreciation before tackling theoretical principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat 'elements' operationally as last terms of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'éléments' pragmatically: substances not yet decomposed by known means are considered elements; do not assert they are absolutely indivisible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that 'elements' may be provisional labels for substances we cannot currently decompose; nomenclature and discussion should reflect this empirical stance rather than metaphysical certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor authorial, experience-based experiments in principal articles
rubrics_metrics.description: In main explanatory sections, rely primarily on experiments personally conducted by the author to illustrate doctrines and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve broader literature summary for compressed reference sections; when opinions or experiments of contemporaries are used without citation, it may reflect shared community practice, but primary articles should be grounded in the author's own work.
